newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - CSX, Norfolk see big growth from Conrail.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CSX, Norfolk see big growth from Conrail.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp. and CSX Corp., which are splitting the prize after a five-month takeover battle for Conrail Inc., said Wednesday the proposed acquisition will sharply boost revenues and earnings over the next several years.

CSX Corp. Chief Financial Officer Paul Goodwin also said the Richmond, Va.-based company anticipates the Surface Transportation Board, the federal agency that oversees railroads, to approve the proposed $10.3 billion transaction early next year.

Both railroads outlined preliminary financial projections in separate conference calls with Wall Street analysts. Both companies said they expected to finance the deal by issuing The purchase will initially dilute earnings for both railroads, but company executives said the division of the East Coast railroad will fuel growth, earnings and cost savings into the next century.

"The transaction is, without any doubt, the right solution for the East and the right solution for the industry as a whole. It's pro-competitive and for the first time in really 30 years, it provides the shippers of the Northeast with two strong, competitive carriers," said CSX Chief Executive Officer John Snow.
Both companies stressed that their financial projections were preliminary, noting that they will provide analysts with more details later this month.

The two railroads late Tuesday released details of how they plan to divide Conrail's assets. A five-month battle for control of Conrail ended last month when the rival bidders agreed to buy Conrail together and split up its key routes.
The proposed transaction calls for Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern to pay $5.9 billion for 58 percent of Conrail and CSX to pay $4.3 billion for 42 percent of the East Coast railroad.

Norfolk Southern Chief Financial Officer Henry Wolf said preliminary projections indicate the proposed transaction will increase the railroad's revenues by more than 50 percent. Norfolk Southern posted a record $4.77 billion in transportation operating revenues in 1996.

"We will have, for the first time, the opportunity to develop a north-south market for both intermodal (rail-and-truck) and conventional traffic and reach fertile new markets as yet untapped," Wolf said in a conference call with Wall Street analysts.

Wolf said the proposed transaction will dilute per-share earnings by 6 percent in 1997 and 1998. It is then expected to boost earnings by 5 percent in 1999, 10 percent in 2000 and more than 15 percent in 2001 and beyond.

The transaction also is expected to result in significant cost savings for Norfolk Southern. The railroad anticipates $90 million of efficiencies in 1998, $220 million in 1999 and $350 million in 2000 and beyond.

Wolf also said the transaction will enable Norfolk Southern to become a major player in the east-west markets between the Midwest and the Northeast and use its Kansas City gateway to provide transcontinental service to the east.

Goodwin of CSX said the railroad expected to achieve efficiencies valued at $75 million in 1998, $170 million in 1999 and $240 million in 2000. Two-thirds of those amounts are expected to come from cost reductions, he said.
Goodwin said the acquisition is expected to lower earnings per share by 1 percent in 1997, have a break-even impact in 1998 and add to earnings by 8 percent in 1999 and 12 percent in 2000.
Shares of Norfolk Southern rose 25 cents to $87.125 on the New York Stock Exchange. CSX gained $1.50 to $45.75, also on NYSE.
